title: FRI Peer Mentor Mindsets Guide
text:
Prologue
Welcome First-year Research Immersion (FRI) Peer Mentors! Thanks for serving the next cohort of students as a mentor during the FRI Semester 1 (Research Methods: HARP 170) course at Binghamton University.
As a peer mentor, you will discover your purpose, adopt a unique mentoring style to support mentees, and develop leadership skills to support your research team. Great mentoring starts with self-awareness: knowing your own mindsets, styles, and preferences so you can adapt to your mentee and team. Each week follows a simple three-step rhythm: a brief mindset lecture or activity, a self-assessment score and reflection, and a journal entry that turns the reflection into a concrete commitment.

title: FRI Peer Mentor Mindsets Guide
text:
A Guide for You
This guide is your companion throughout the semester. Each week, you will learn about a new mindset related to peer mentoring, review your score on that mindset, and discuss how to answer the big question of the week. Each chapter has the distribution for that week’s measure and a password lookup table where you can find your own score(s).








Week
Mindset
Big Question




1
Mentoring Style
Does your style focus on structure or support?


2
Motivational Style
Is your motivational approach to promote or prevent for academics or social connection?


3
Leadership Focus
Is your leadership style to promote or prevent for the team?


4
Feedback Orientation
Is your feedback preference supportive or corrective?


5
Feedback Purpose
Is your feedback preference developmental or summative?


6
Leadership Role
Is your team’s leadership positional or shared?


7
Leadership Target
Is your leadership style task or relational oriented?


8
Inclusive Mentoring
Is your mentoring inclusive?


9
Conflict Mediator
What is your conflict resolution style?


10
Goal Preference
What is your goal orientation?


11
Communicator
What is your communication style?


12
People Orientation
What is your view of people?


13
Self-Awareness
What is your self-awareness type?




How to find your scores
At the end of the anonymous survey you created a password. Each chapter contains a table where you look up your password to find your composite scores for that week’s measure.






NoteSave your password



Your password is the key to your individual scores all semester. Keep it in your phone notes. To change it, contact the course instructor.




How to interpret your scores
Each measure produces a composite score, the average of your responses to a set of related items (after adjusting any reverse-coded items so all point the same way).

Find your score in the password lookup table.
Locate it on the class distribution. The dashed lines mark the 33rd and 67th percentiles, and the shaded bands show the Low / Mid / High thirds of the class.
Compare where you fall relative to your peers.
Reflect using the two prompts at the end of each chapter.







NoteThere are no right or wrong scores



These measures capture orientations and styles, not ability. The purpose is self-awareness.








ImportantAbout the data



Every score, table, and figure in this draft is simulated for layout and review. Real results will replace them once the pre/post Qualtrics survey is collected.


The first numbered chapter, 1. Mentoring Style, begins the weekly measures.

title: 1. Mentoring Style
text:
The Mindset(s)
Does your style focus on structure or support?
Authoritative mentoring blends two things at once:
Polarity: Structure ↔︎ Support.
Measure: Mentoring Style Values Inventory (importance-rated; adapted from Ertesvåg, 2011). Eight items, four per subscale, rated 1–10 for importance under a 40-point budget that forces you to prioritize.

title: 1. Mentoring Style
text:
Support: warmth, care, and responsiveness toward your mentees.

Survey item: “How important is it to you, as a mentor, to build good relationships with your mentees?”

Structure: clear routines, expectations, and follow-through.

Survey item: “How important is it to you, as a mentor, to set clear expectations for how your team works together?”

title: 1. Mentoring Style
text:
Your Type
Structure and support are two dimensions that result in four mentoring styles. Neither dimension is “good” or “bad” on its own; it is the combination that describes how you show up as a mentor:









Low Support
High Support




High Structure
Authoritarian: high expectations, little warmth. Clear and demanding, but mentees may not feel safe asking for help.
Authoritative: high expectations and high warmth. Clear structure that mentees experience as being on their side.


Low Structure
Uninvolved: low on both. Mentees are largely left to themselves.
Permissive: warm and caring, but loose on expectations. Mentees feel supported but may drift.

Your Mentoring Style
Each dot is one peer mentor. The dashed lines are the class medians on each dimension, so “high” and “low” here mean relative to your classmates, not relative to the 1–10 scale. Almost everyone rates both dimensions as important, so a scale-midpoint split would put the whole class in one corner. Find your Style in the table above, then find your quadrant.















NoteYour style is a snapshot, not a fixed type



The median split means roughly a quarter of the class lands in each quadrant by construction. If you sit close to a dashed line, small changes in a few answers would move you. Each quadrant is a rough approximation of your balance between structure and support. This is not a fixed type! You can change your attention and behaviors to move from one quadrant to another over time.

title: 2. Motivational Style
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is your motivational approach to promote or prevent for academics or social connection?
Regulatory focus crosses two dimensions. The focus is what you are steering toward, and the goal is what you are hoping to attain.
Polarity: Promotion ↔︎ Prevention × Academic ↔︎ Social.
Measure: Mentoring Regulatory Focus Scale, 2×2 (adapted; Higgins, 1997; Lockwood, Jordan & Kunda, 2002). Twelve items rated 1–9, three per cell. Focus and referent are scored separately.

title: 2. Motivational Style
text:
Promotion: oriented toward gains, growth, and what your mentees could become.

Survey item: “I see myself as someone who helps my mentees reach their full potential as researchers.”

Prevention: oriented toward safety, avoiding mistakes, and what could go wrong.

Survey item: “I often think about how I can prevent problems from derailing my mentees’ research.”

Academic referent: your team’s research project.

Survey item: “Right now, I am focused on helping my mentees make progress and grow in their research project.”

Social referent: belonging to the team and connections on campus.

Survey item: “Right now, I am focused on helping my mentees build a sense of belonging and connection on the team.”

title: 2. Motivational Style
text:
Your Motivational Style
Each dot is one peer mentor. These two plots split your motivation into how strongly you hold a focus and what you aim it at.
The horizontal axis is how strongly you hold that focus overall. The dashed line is the class median, so “high” and “low” mean relative to your classmates, not relative to the 1–9 scale. The vertical axis is a difference score: how much more you aim that focus at academic goals (your team’s research project) than at social goals (belonging and connection). Here the solid line at zero is a real anchor, not a class comparison. Above it you lean academic, below it you lean social, and on it you weight the two equally. Find your Promotion aim and Prevention aim in the table above.
























NoteYour style is a snapshot, not a fixed type



The median split on the horizontal axis means roughly half the class sits on each side by construction. If you sit close to either line, small changes in a few answers would move you. The two plots are also independent: a strong promotion focus does not imply a weak prevention focus, and you can aim them at different goals. Read your position as a description of your current balance, not a fixed type.

title: 3. Leadership Focus
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is your leadership style to promote or prevent for the team?
The same regulatory focus from Week 2, now applied to how you lead. Each pole covers the same four leadership functions: goal framing, problem solving, error management, and feedback.
Polarity: Promotion ↔︎ Prevention (team leadership).
Measure: Promotion/Prevention Team Leadership Scale (adapted from regulatory focus theory). Eight items rated 1–9, four per subscale.

title: 3. Leadership Focus
text:
Promotion Leadership: frames goals around gains, builds on what works, encourages useful risks, and affirms what is going well.

Survey item: “I motivate my team by framing our goals around the gains and growth we can achieve.”

Prevention Leadership: frames goals around setbacks to avoid, fixes what is going wrong, emphasizes accuracy, and corrects errors.

Survey item: “I motivate my team by framing our goals around the problems and setbacks we need to avoid.”

title: 4. Feedback Orientation
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is your feedback preference supportive or corrective?
Feedback orientation is a single bipolar dimension. It is not about how much feedback you give, but about which way you lean when you give it. Neither end is better; mentees need both, and the useful skill is knowing which one a moment calls for.
Polarity: Corrective ↔︎ Supportive.
Measure: Feedback Orientation, bipolar (author-created for this course). Three semantic-differential items rated 1–7, where 1 = fully corrective and 7 = fully supportive. Your score is the mean of the three items, so 4 is balanced, below 4 leans corrective, and above 4 leans supportive.

title: 4. Feedback Orientation
text:
Corrective (the low end): feedback aimed at what needs fixing, the gap between the work and the standard.

Survey item: “I focus on mistakes to correct” (vs. “I focus on strengths to build on”).

Supportive (the high end): feedback aimed at affirming and encouraging, building on what is already working.

Survey item: “My instinct is to affirm and encourage” (vs. “My instinct is to close the gap to the standard”).

title: 5. Feedback Purpose
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is your feedback preference developmental or summative?
Polarity: Surface ↔︎ Substantive; Developmental ↔︎ Summative.
Measure: Dual-Role Feedback Orientation Scale · giving-feedback (2025); Teachers’ Conceptions of Assessment · Improvement vs. Accountability (Brown, 2006).

title: 5. Feedback Purpose
text:
Surface ↔︎ Substantive: whether feedback addresses presentation and mechanics or the underlying reasoning.

Survey item: items pending.

title: 6. Leadership Role
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is your team’s leadership positional or shared?
Polarity: Positional/Formal ↔︎ Shared/Informal.
Measure: SPLIT, full inventory (Grille & Kauffeld, 2015; cf. Hiller et al., 2006).

title: 6. Leadership Role
text:
Positional / formal leadership: leadership that comes from an assigned role and sits with one person.

Survey item: items pending.

Shared / informal leadership: leadership that is distributed across the team and emerges from the work.

Survey item: items pending.










NoteMeasure pending



The full SPLIT adds change-oriented and micropolitical subscales beyond the task and relation subscales you complete in Week 7. Those items have not yet been sourced.

title: 7. Leadership Target
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is your leadership style task or relational oriented?
SPLIT is a team-referent measure: it asks how much the team as a whole shares leadership, not how much you personally lead. Every item begins “As a team we…”.
Polarity: Task ↔︎ Relational.
Measure: SPLIT · task and relation subscales (Grille & Kauffeld, 2015). Ten items, five per subscale, rated 0–100.

title: 7. Leadership Target
text:
Task leadership: the team assigns work, communicates expectations, and tracks whether goals are met.

Survey item: “As a team we clearly assign tasks.”

Relational leadership: the team attends to concerns, recognizes good work, builds cohesion, and handles conflict.

Survey item: “As a team we take sufficient time to address each other’s concerns.”

title: 9. Conflict Mediator
text:
The Mindset(s)
What is your conflict resolution style?
Conflict is simply the condition where two people’s concerns appear incompatible. It is not the same as fighting, and it is not automatically destructive. Two dimensions describe how you handle it: assertiveness (how far you try to satisfy your own concerns) and cooperativeness (how far you try to satisfy the other person’s). Crossing them gives five styles. No style is wrong. Each one works well in some situations and costs you in others.
Polarity: Win/Avoid ↔︎ Understand/Resolve, across five styles.
Measure: Dutch Test for Conflict Handling (DUTCH; De Dreu, Evers, Beersma, Kluwer & Nauta, 2001), short form. Fifteen items, three per style, rated 1 = Not at all to 5 = Very much. Each style is scored as the mean of its three items, so you get a profile across all five rather than a single label.

title: 9. Conflict Mediator
text:
Competing: assertive and uncooperative. You pursue your own concerns at the other person’s expense.

Survey item: “I push my own point of view.”

Collaborating: assertive and cooperative. You look for a win-win that completely satisfies both people’s concerns.

Survey item: “I examine issues until I find a solution that really satisfies me and the other party.”

Compromising: intermediate on both. You find an acceptable solution that only partly satisfies both people’s concerns.

Survey item: “I try to realize a middle-of-the-road solution.”

Avoiding: unassertive and uncooperative. You sidestep the conflict without trying to satisfy either person’s concerns.

Survey item: “I avoid confrontation about our differences.”

Accommodating: unassertive and cooperative. You satisfy the other person’s concerns at the expense of your own.

Survey item: “I give in to the wishes of the other party.”

title: 9. Conflict Mediator
text:
Your Type
Every mode has benefits and costs. The skill is knowing when to use each one, not defaulting to a favorite.








Style
Works well when
Costs you when




Competing
The issue is critical, you are clearly right, or a fast decision is needed
Overused: strained relationships, worse decisions, less buy-in from your team


Collaborating
The stakes are high enough to justify the time and both sets of concerns matter
The issue is trivial, or there is no time


Compromising
You need a workable answer quickly and both sides can give a little
It becomes the reflex, and nobody’s real concern gets met


Avoiding
The issue is minor, tempers are hot, or you need time to gather information
The problem festers and your mentees read the silence as indifference


Accommodating
You are wrong, the issue matters far more to them, or preserving the relationship is the priority
Your own concerns disappear and your credibility erodes









NoteOn the measure



The five styles come from the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (TKI) framework. The TKI itself is commercially licensed, so this guide uses the DUTCH, a published and validated instrument covering the same five styles, drawn from concern-for-self and concern-for-others. Items are verbatim; the short form uses three of the four to five items per style, so reliability should be re-checked on this sample before results are reported anywhere beyond this guide.

The Mindset(s)
What is your communication style?
Nonviolent Communication describes three behaviors that keep a hard conversation connected rather than combative.
Polarity: Violent ↔︎ Nonviolent.

title: 11. Communicator
text:
Self-connection: recognizing that your emotions come from your own thoughts and unmet needs, and staying present enough under stress to notice a reaction without acting on it.

Survey item: “Knowing that my emotions stem from my own thoughts and unmet needs, my emotions are not caused by others.”

Authentic self-expression: stating your feelings, needs, and requests sincerely, without accusation, and staying open to any response.

Survey item: “Being responsible for my own experience, and willing to express my feelings and needs sincerely without accusation or criticism.”

Empathic listening: staying open and flexible, and using conflict to connect rather than to win.

Survey item: “Listen patiently, try to understand other people from their perspective.”

title: 12. People Orientation
text:
The Mindset(s)
What is your view of people?
An implicit theory is your working assumption about whether people can change. It matters for mentoring because it shapes how you read a struggling mentee.
Polarity: Fixed ↔︎ Growth.
Measure: ‘Kind of Person’ Implicit Theory Scale (Dweck, 1999). Eight items rated 1–6. Fixed-mindset items are reverse-scored, so a higher composite means a stronger growth mindset.

title: 12. People Orientation
text:
Growth orientation: people’s basic characteristics can substantially change.

Survey item: “Everyone, no matter who they are, can significantly change their basic characteristics.”

Fixed orientation: the important parts of who someone is cannot really be changed.

Survey item: “The kind of person someone is, is something very basic about them and it can’t be changed very much.”

title: 13. Self-Awareness
text:
The Mindset(s)
What is your self-awareness type?
Dr. Tasha Eurich conceptualized this self-awareness model and its four types, based on a large-scale research program reported in Insight (2017) and in the Harvard Business Review (Eurich, 2018). Her team found that self-awareness splits into two dimensions that are largely unrelated to each other: being high on one says almost nothing about the other. Most people believe they are self-aware; Eurich estimates only 10 to 15% actually meet the criteria.
Polarity: Internal ↔︎ External self-awareness.
Measure: Self-Reflection & Insight Scale · Insight (Grant, Franklin & Langford, 2002) for the internal dimension; MCA · Fostering Independence (Fleming et al., 2013). Eurich’s model is a framework, not a published self-report scale, so the external dimension still needs a sourced instrument.

title: 13. Self-Awareness
text:
Internal self-awareness: how clearly you see your own values, passions, aspirations, reactions, strengths and weaknesses, and your impact on others.

Survey item: items pending.

External self-awareness: how well you understand the way other people actually see you, on those same factors.

Survey item: items pending.

title: 13. Self-Awareness
text:
Your Type
Crossing the two dimensions gives Eurich’s four self-awareness types. As in Week 1, the useful move is not picking a side but raising both:









Low External
High External




High Internal
Introspectors: clear on who they are, but they do not challenge their own views or seek feedback, so blind spots persist.
Aware: know who they are and what they want, and actively seek and value how others see them.


Low Internal
Seekers: do not yet know who they are, what they stand for, or how their team sees them. Often feel stuck or frustrated.
Pleasers: so focused on how they come across that they lose track of what matters to them, and drift into choices that do not serve them.









NoteMeasure pending



The MCA · Fostering Independence items are already collected at Kickoff. The SRIS · Insight items have not yet been sourced, and no instrument has been selected for the external dimension.

title: 13. Self-Awareness
text:
Reflect and Plan






WarningJournal




Score: Which of the four types best describes you right now, and what would move you toward Aware?
Behavior: To be the best mentor you can be, what is one new thing you will try to do this week for mentees and/or your team?









TipUGPM Meeting



Both dimensions are trainable, and they are trained differently. Internal self-awareness grows through better introspection. Eurich’s research found that asking “what” rather than “why” is what makes introspection productive: “why” invites rationalizing, “what” points at something you can act on. External self-awareness grows only by asking people who will tell you the truth.
